analysis.one_liner: Requires credit bureaus to disclose data breaches, give victims free credit freezes, and face fines.
analysis.headline: The bill got no cosponsors, never received a committee hearing or vote, and died in the House Financial Services Committee when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Fair Credit Reporting Act to force consumer reporting agencies — the companies that keep credit files on nearly every American adult — to tell regulators within two days and affected individuals within three days of a data breach [S2][S3]. Breached agencies would have had to give victims free credit freezes and credit monitoring for life, staff a free consumer assistance unit for ten years, and face civil penalties of up to $2,500 per affected person, plus private lawsuits by victims [S3]. It also barred agencies from making consumers sign away their right to sue as a condition of getting services [S3]. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never moved again [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone whose sensitive personal information sits in a credit bureau's files and could be exposed in a breach: they would get fast notification, free credit freezes and monitoring, a free dispute-assistance unit, and the right to sue for at least $1,000 in damages plus attorney's fees [S3]. Regulators would gain authority to examine the agencies' data security and penalize breaches [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People exposed by credit bureau breaches

how_it_helps.text: A consumer reporting agency that suffers a data breach must notify the FTC, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, law enforcement within two days, and every affected individual within three days [S2][S3].
Affected individuals can get free credit freezes and free credit monitoring for life, and the agency must fund a free consumer assistance unit for ten years to help dispute fraudulent entries [S3].

Victims gain a private right to sue for actual losses or $1,000 in liquidated damages, plus punitive damages and attorney's fees, and the agency cannot force them to waive these rights or accept settlement inducements [S3].

The CFPB may examine consumer reporting agencies for compliance with data-security standards, and the FTC or CFPB can seek civil penalties of up to $2,500 per affected individual for negligent or knowing breaches [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The consumer reporting agencies would bear the direct cost: breach notification, free credit freezes and monitoring, a ten-year consumer assistance unit, civil penalties up to $25 million per breach, and private lawsuit payouts, some of which could be passed along through the price of credit products [S3].

drawbacks.text: The total civil penalty is capped at $25 million regardless of how many people were affected, a ceiling that a large agency could treat as an affordable cost of doing business [S3].

Two- and three-day notification deadlines could strain incident response, and extension is available only for national-security reasons, not for the operational difficulty of determining breach scope [S3].
Compliance, freeze, and monitoring costs would be borne by the agencies, and some of that cost could be passed on to consumers through the price of credit products [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the public, the benefits are concrete: fast notice, free freezes and monitoring, a way to sue, and real regulatory oversight of companies that hold nearly every American's most sensitive financial data. The main honest criticisms are that the $25 million penalty cap is small relative to the scale of a major breach, and the deadlines are aggressive. Those are design quibbles, not reasons the bill failed — it never got a hearing or a single cosponsor, so its merits were never weighed on the floor [S4][S5].

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced, got zero cosponsors, and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended [S1][S4][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Albio Sires introduced the Consumer Data Protection Act on December 4, 2017, and it was immediately referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1][S5].
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumer reporting agencies are better off: they never had to accept fast breach disclosure, free lifetime freezes and monitoring, regulator examinations, fines, or a private right of action for breach victims [S3]. Consumers whose data a bureau loses remain without the federal protections this bill would have created [S3].

for.name: Rep. Albio Sires
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Financial Services Committee.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: House committee of jurisdiction over consumer credit and credit reporting law
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on December 4, 2017 and never reported it out, held no hearing on it, and let it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no other member signed on, so the partisan shape of opposition never showed up in the record — only the single Democratic sponsor's support is visible [S4].

industries.industry: Consumer credit reporting agencies (the companies that hold Americans' credit files)
industries.note: The bill would have imposed fast breach disclosure, free lifetime credit freezes and monitoring, a ten-year free assistance unit, CFPB examinations, fines up to $25 million, and victims' lawsuits on these agencies [S3]. Their gain from the bill's death is the continued absence of those obligations — costs and liabilities that fall on the public when their data is exposed.

industries.industry: Credit monitoring and identity-theft protection providers
industries.note: Free, mandatory credit monitoring from the breached agency would have substituted for paid monitoring services consumers otherwise buy after a breach [S3].
